doc.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Rivalry and comparison with Oscar Peterson
summary: A critic said she played as well as Peterson; she calls herself more versatile and sees him as a Nat Cole and Earl Hines disciple rather than Tatum's.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: (I want to) ask you about another experience at Carnegie Hall with Oscar Peterson. I understand there was a little bit of competition or rivalry, at least on his side, and not necessarily wanting to play after you. Can you tell me about that experience?

Did I play first? Or did he play first? The critic, John Wilson, said that my runs had come more to the point that his, that I enjoyed no popularity, they thought I should be reckoned in the same light that he is. They said that I had played just as well, maybe better.
Do you think of Oscar Peterson as your closest competition?
Sometimes I say that I’m more versatile than he is (laughs). He’s more predictable but he’s a great pianist. And he’s lost his left hand.
It’s the stroke. What do you most admire about Oscar Peterson?
He’s got a nice touch. He’s a big man of the piano, a giant.
He’s also an Art Tatum protégée.
No, he’s a Nat Cole protégée.
Interesting. Tell me about that. Take that a little bit further.
He heard Earl Hines first. So, he patterned his style after Earl Hines and Nat Cole. And he sings too.
